content:
You look out at the world and it’s not the most appealing picture.

There’s selfishness. Greed. Incompetence. People suffering. Problems that desperately need solving…and the very obvious and necessary solutions getting ignored.

I see that and I get discouraged. I get cynical. I lose hope.

But if I take a different view, I have a very different reaction.

Go to your local food bank, and you will see volunteers spending their Saturday packing boxes for families they don’t know. Go to a blood drive, and you will see people rolling up their sleeves to give blood that could save the life of someone they’ll never meet. Go to a nursing home, and you will see people spending their afternoon making a stranger feel a little less alone. Go somewhere like the Naval Academy or West Point and see the very best of a generation, who could have enrolled at any elite university in the country and they chose to go there.

When I see these things, I get inspired. I get hopeful. But most of all, I get moving.

I want to be like those people. I want to do something.

This is what philosophy is, by the way, changing your view on something—the lens you are using—so you can change your actions.

Going back to my days at American Apparel, I’d always disliked the commercialism of Thanksgiving and Christmas—at least here in the US. I hated that every year, businesses seemed expected to offer bigger and bigger sales for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, starting earlier and earlier. I hated reading about people getting trampled by crowds rushing into stores to get a deal. I hated seeing all the clips of people fighting over flat-screen televisions, yelling at employees, tearing apart displays, and overturning racks of clothes.

I think that’s one view and it’s a pretty hard one to miss.

But then I saw a story that helped me see another. REI, starting in 2015, announced it was closing its stores every Black Friday and paying its tens of thousands of employees to enjoy the day off outdoors with family and friends. I learned that Patagonia was running a Black Friday fundraiser in 2019, raising $10 million in donations from tens of thousands of people, which the company matched, donating the $20 million to various environmental organizations. I learned about a shop in London, where people line up, patiently and orderly, on Black Friday to buy sleeping bags, warm coats and blankets for refugees.

Change your view…change your actions.

In 2020, I talked to everyone on the Daily Stoic team about their interest in doing something like that. Black Friday and Cyber Monday were two of the biggest sales days of the year—for our business but for most businesses—what if we used that for good instead? So that year, on Black Friday and Cyber Monday, we ran a fundraiser for Feeding America, a nonprofit that helps provide meals to families experiencing hunger. I put in the first $10,000, and with the help of Daily Stoic readers, we raised over $100,000. The next year, we did it again. And every year since. Cumulatively, we’ve raised over $1 million, helping provide 10 million meals for people in need.

Did it save the world? Of course not. But it definitely made some people’s worlds a little better. And you know what else? It made me and my world better too.

Seeing all these people who chipped in $5 or $10…or in some cases, $1,000…flipped me. I went from losing my faith in humanity to being an absolute believer in how decent and generous people can be. I became optimistic about the potential for people to come together and solve tough problems (and hunger is a very real problem). Imagine, an organization can provide ten meals for a $1? How cool is that?! And it got me excited about using my platform and my business to do more things that were good.

This is why how you look at things matters so much. It doesn’t change what is or what’s happened. But it does change what you do.

Yes, there is a lot of selfishness in this world. A lot of cruelty. People who take more than they need and give less than they could. People who see suffering and look the other way.

And yet.

And yet there is so much good in the world too. So much selflessness. So many inspiring people. So many givers and helpers. That’s the famous Mr. Rogers line: “Look for the helpers.”

Who are you looking for? Which picture are you seeing? Which handle—to borrow Epictetus’ phrase—are you grabbing. The one that makes you hopeless or hopeful? Passive or active? Disgusted or inspired?

But the important thing is that you don’t just look at the helpers, it’s that you look at them and then follow their lead.

This year we are once again teaming up with Feeding America to help hungry and struggling families.

We donated the first $40,000 and I’d love your help in getting to our goal of $400,000—which would provide over 4 million meals for families across the country! (Just head over to feedingamerica.org/dailystoic—every dollar provides 10 meals, even a small donation makes a big difference.)

The point is: It’s on us.

We can choose what we focus on.

We can choose what we see.

And most importantly, we can choose whose example we are going to follow in—what picture we are going to help paint.
